quotes.verbatim_quote: Use the thumb (p) to play the lower three open strings, E, A and D.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the foundational rule assigning the right-hand thumb to bass strings, which governs all subsequent two-part fingerstyle texture in the method.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In simple fingerstyle guitar notation, notes
with down-pointing stems indicate the use of thumb, free stroke.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the notational convention used throughout the entire book to distinguish thumb (bass) from finger (melody) parts.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
For the next exercise, play the top part (stems up) played /-m, rest stroke, and the bottom part
(stems down) with p, free stroke. When alternating strokes between fingers and thumb, don't let your
right hand be pulled out of alignment.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage introduces the core right-hand coordination challenge of fingerstyle jazz -- maintaining hand alignment while alternating between rest-stroke fingers and free-stroke thumb.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
RH: Use rest stroke with /, m, or a for notes with stems pointing up and free stroke with p for
notes with stems pointing down. Your fingering may emphasize assigning fingers to strings, one
per string. Using a fixed pair such as i-m or m-a for the notes with stems pointing up would work
also. So would mixing and matching.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives the student explicit permission and guidance to choose among multiple valid fingering strategies, framing the decision as a deliberate choice rather than a fixed rule.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Remember to keep the left thumb under the neck and fingers arched over the fretboard. Fretted
notes allow you to have more control over duration, tone and expression.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This states the canonical left-hand position rule and connects it to musical outcomes (duration, tone, expression), making it both a technique instruction and a motivating principle.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Blues has a form. The most common form is twelve measures long with a standard harmonic
structure (chords). In the following blues exercise, chord symbols are above the melody to indicate
when the harmony changes.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the method's first definition of blues form, establishing the twelve-bar structure and the relationship between melody and chord symbols before the student plays their first full blues.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Here is the complete blues scale in an ascending and descending pattern. The scale begins
and ends on E eight lines or spaces above. In this exercise, the scale returns to where it started.
This distance is an octave. Memorize this scale. It’s called the E minor pentatonic blues scale.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the chapter's central scale definition -- naming, describing, and commanding memorization of the E minor pentatonic blues scale, which underlies all the blues exercises that follow.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
After you play a fretted note, stop it
from ringing further by releasing the
pressure of the active finger.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the fundamental technique rule for executing rests on fretted notes, the simplest case that the method builds on before introducing open-string damping.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
If a sounding open string needs to stop at a specific moment,
as when it is followed by a rest, damp it by touching it very lightly with a free finger. For now, start
with any free right-hand finger.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This introduces the open-string damping technique, a critical skill for rhythmic precision in fingerstyle guitar that differs fundamentally from stopping a fretted note.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Practice damping the open string with the next finger in the normal alternation pattern. If
you’ve just used /to pluck an open note, use mto damp the open note on the beat of the rest. Just
pretend you are going to pluck the note again, swing into it lightly and just touch it.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives a specific, actionable rule for which finger to use when damping, integrating damping seamlessly into the existing i-m alternation technique.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The right thumb (p) will need damping skills too. Begin with using it both to play and damp
notes. As before, the open string before a rest is the one that will need damping.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This extends the damping concept to the thumb, completing the picture of right-hand muting across all fingers and establishing that both bass and treble voices require active silence.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Atie symbol joins notes of the same
pitch. The note on the left continues sounding for
the duration of the note on the right. Do not pluck
the second note. The combination of two tied
quarter notes, below, sustains for a total of two
beats. Notes can be tied within a measure or
between measures.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the method's formal definition of the tie, a notation concept essential for reading two-part fingerstyle arrangements where sustained inner voices must be distinguished from repeated attacks.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When music is divided into two parts—melody and accompaniment—the number of beats
per measure in each part must add up to the number of beats indicated in the time signature.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This states the governing rule of two-part notation that the student must internalize before writing or reading any solo jazz guitar arrangement.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Having notes on lower strings does not by itself mean that they are automatically
played with the thumb. If music has only one part (melody or accompaniment) paired /-m fingers
will often play across all strings. If there are big jumps across strings, the thumb will enter to play.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This corrects a likely student assumption by articulating the rule that string assignment -- not string position -- determines whether thumb or fingers play, a foundational principle for single-line jazz melodies.
